number-theory.body:
Why is $13=2^2+3^2$, while 11 cannot be written as a sum of two integer squares? Reducing squares modulo 4 rules out 11 immediately: a square leaves remainder 0 or 1. Proving that every prime congruent to 1 modulo 4 is a sum of two squares requires a more substantial idea. This movement between a calculation, an obstruction, and a general existence theorem is characteristic of number theory. It also explains why elementary questions can lead toward algebra, analysis, or geometry without any one of those subjects supplying the whole story.

A good first spine is William Stein's [Elementary Number Theory: Primes, Congruences, and Secrets](https://wstein.org/ent/ent.pdf). Begin with Chapters 1 and 2, especially the Chinese remainder theorem in Section 2.2. Solve a pair of congruences by hand, then explain why the solution is unique modulo the product when the moduli are coprime. Continue to Chapter 4 on quadratic reciprocity; Section 5.7 returns to sums of two squares. This gives a connected project rather than a collection of unrelated tricks. The computational examples are useful experiments, but the proofs explain which patterns persist.

You can start the arithmetic with induction, divisibility, and some experience writing proofs. Stein assumes some basic abstract algebra for the book as a whole, so keep quotient rings, finite groups, and fields available for review. To decide whether to skip the opening material, try proving Bézout's identity, finding an inverse modulo 35 when it exists, and explaining why cancellation modulo a composite number needs a hypothesis. If these are routine, move to reciprocity or continued fractions. If they are not, a short return to the Euclidean algorithm will be more useful than pushing through unfamiliar notation.

The algebraic branch asks what happens when integers are replaced by algebraic integers. In $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, the two decompositions $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ suggest that familiar factorization arguments need repair. James S. Milne's [Algebraic Number Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf) supplies a later route: use Chapter 1 to identify missing commutative algebra, then study Chapter 2 on rings of integers and Chapter 3 on Dedekind domains and ideal factorization. Before beginning, you should be able to use ideals, quotient rings, and finite field extensions in examples. Calculate in a quadratic field alongside the general theory; otherwise ideals can become names for a repair you have never seen working.

An analytic direction starts from different questions: how many primes lie below a large bound, or how evenly are they distributed among residue classes? Here estimates, series, and complex functions become central. Prepare real and complex analysis for this branch as those tools arise. Completing algebraic number theory first is unnecessary. Conversely, familiarity with congruences does not make contour integration or convergence arguments automatic. Choose a first analytic project small enough that you can distinguish an exact identity from an asymptotic statement and identify the error being controlled.

For a connection with geometry, Milne's [Modular Functions and Modular Forms](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/MF.pdf) offers a later alternative. Read its introduction for motivation, then the preliminaries and the discussion of modular curves as Riemann surfaces before Section 4 on modular forms. Its stated preparation includes advanced undergraduate algebra and complex analysis. The boundary conditions at cusps matter just as much as the transformation formula; ignoring them changes the objects under study.

Keep a notebook of worked examples and failed conjectures: noncoprime congruences, quadratic residues for small primes, and competing factorizations. For each theorem, record where its hypotheses enter. Then choose a next branch by the question you want to answer: continued fractions for approximation, ideals and valuations for arithmetic in fields, analytic estimates for distribution, or elliptic curves and modular forms for arithmetic geometry. There is no need to turn these branches into one compulsory reading sequence.

logic.body:
Suppose someone proposes a collection of first-order axioms whose models are exactly the finite structures. For each positive integer $n$, add a sentence saying that at least $n$ distinct objects exist. Any finite portion of the enlarged collection still has a model: choose a sufficiently large finite structure. Compactness would then produce a model satisfying the entire collection, which would have to be both finite and infinite. The contradiction reveals a limitation of first-order axiomatization. Logic studies such limitations by making languages, interpretations, and proofs into mathematical objects in their own right.

For the main route, use Richard Zach's [Sets, Logic, Computation](https://slc.openlogicproject.org/slc-screen.pdf). It connects the set-theoretic language needed to discuss formal systems with first-order syntax, semantics, derivations, and the completeness theorem. Work toward Chapter 12, particularly Sections 12.8–12.11 on completeness, compactness, and Löwenheim–Skolem. The opening example becomes a worthwhile destination: reconstruct the argument with an explicit sentence for each lower bound on the size of the domain. Notice that compactness concerns satisfiability of finite subsets of sentences; it is not a claim about compact topological spaces made without further translation.

This book is an introduction to metalogic and expects some prior formal logic. Test that preparation by translating a sentence with alternating quantifiers, negating it correctly, and giving an interpretation in which it is false. You should also be able to distinguish a formula with a free variable from a sentence, and a derivation from a truth-table calculation. Readers who need that practice can start with [forall x: Calgary](https://forallx.openlogicproject.org/html/), by P. D. Magnus, Tim Button, Robert Trueman, and Richard Zach. Parts V–VII develop first-order language, interpretations, and natural deduction. Its earlier parts provide a slower entry through arguments and truth-functional logic.

The two books serve different purposes. Use forall x when the immediate difficulty is choosing a quantifier, understanding an interpretation, or applying a deduction rule. Use Sets, Logic, Computation when you can perform those operations and want to prove general facts about them. If ordinary set notation, functions, and relations are already comfortable, sample the opening exercises and skip the corresponding review. Keep structural induction in view: a formula is built recursively, so proofs about every formula often follow its construction. This is a more useful readiness test than knowing a long list of logical symbols.

Work on a tiny language throughout the course. Take one binary relation and interpret it as an order on two or three objects. Write a sentence asserting transitivity, construct a counterinterpretation, and compare semantic validity with derivability in the chosen calculus. Later, interpret the same formal language in an infinite structure. Small examples make the distinction between symbols and their meanings tangible, while infinite examples show why metatheorems have consequences beyond mechanical proof checking.

After completeness, the route divides. Model theory follows the relationship between theories and their structures; compactness is an early working tool, and groups or fields supply useful examples once abstract algebra is available. Computability follows the possibility and limits of algorithms; the later Turing-machine and undecidability material in Zach's text provides a continuation. Set theory asks about axioms governing sets, ordinals, cardinals, and constructions of mathematical universes. The opening naive set theory supports the common language, but further axiomatic set theory requires a separate sustained course. Algebra is helpful for one branch rather than an entrance requirement for all three.

Two confusions are especially costly. Completeness of first-order logic is different from completeness of a particular theory, and a theorem proved about a formal calculus is different from a theorem proved inside it. Keep separate pages for a system's rules and the mathematical arguments establishing properties of that system. A productive next step is to apply one metatheorem to an unfamiliar example and write out every hypothesis. That turns foundational vocabulary into a usable method.

probability.body:
A fair coin has no memory, yet its running proportion of heads settles near one half. What exactly does that mean? A statement about the probability of a large error at time $n$ differs from a statement about almost every infinite sequence of tosses. Neither says that heads and tails must balance after a bad run. The passage from elementary probability to measure-theoretic probability begins when these distinctions become part of the question, rather than technical qualifications added after a calculation.

If distributions, expectation, and conditioning are new, start with Charles M. Grinstead and J. Laurie Snell's [Introduction to Probability](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~doyle/docs/prob/prob.pdf), in the freely available CHANCE Project version. Chapters 1–2 introduce discrete and continuous models; Chapters 4 and 6 develop conditioning and expectation. Then compare Chapter 8 on laws of large numbers with Chapter 9 on central limit theorems. Keep the coin experiment beside the theory: estimate a tail probability, simulate several sample paths if useful, and ask which mathematical statement each picture could illustrate. A plot supplies examples, while a proof controls all the relevant outcomes at once.

You can skip much of this opening if you can calculate an expectation from a distribution, use conditional probability without reversing the conditioning event, and derive the variance of a sum of independent variables. Try those tasks before deciding that another introductory book is needed. Calculus supports continuous distributions, and elementary counting supports discrete ones. For the next stage, add rigorous analysis: sequences of functions, countable operations on sets, and Lebesgue integration. Being quick with densities is useful preparation, but probability measures also describe discrete laws and mixtures that have no density with respect to ordinary length.

The destination text is Rick Durrett's [Probability: Theory and Examples](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf), fifth-edition author PDF. Chapter 1 develops the measure and integration framework; Chapters 2–3 address laws of large numbers and central limit theorems. Readers who already know measure theory can test themselves on measurable random variables and convergence theorems, then move directly into probabilistic arguments. Readers meeting integration for the first time should work examples slowly and use the opening chapter as a guide to the analysis they need. A short review cannot replace practice applying monotone and dominated convergence with their hypotheses visible.

A useful exercise is to define $X_n$ on $[0,1]$ to equal $n$ on $(0,1/n)$ and zero elsewhere, with uniform probability. For each fixed point, $X_n$ eventually vanishes, but its expectation remains one. Explain why moving a limit through an expectation fails here. Then modify the example so that $|X_n|\leq M$ for one constant $M$ independent of $n$, while retaining pointwise convergence to zero, and check what happens to the expectations. This small calculation exposes a recurring issue in probability: the rare outcomes can become larger while their probabilities shrink. It also gives you something concrete to recall when a proof asks for integrability or uniform control.

From there, choose the next question. Durrett's Chapter 4 develops conditional expectation and martingales. For an integrable variable, conditioning on a sigma-algebra produces another random variable that reflects the information retained; it need not reduce to dividing two event probabilities. Start with a finite partition and compute the average on each piece before attempting the abstract definition. If finite-state evolution is more appealing, Grinstead and Snell's Chapter 11 offers a Markov-chain route with matrix calculations. These are meaningful alternatives: one emphasizes information and conditional averages, the other transitions between states.

Keep a comparison sheet for almost sure convergence, convergence in probability, convergence in distribution, and convergence in mean. Supply examples and counterexamples as each appears. Before using a limit theorem, name its assumptions and the quantity being normalized. Later branches include Brownian motion, stochastic integration, interacting systems, and links with ergodic theory. Choose one after you can carry a complete argument from a probabilistic model through its measure-theoretic formulation to a justified conclusion.

dynamics.body:
Choose a number $x_0$ between zero and one and repeat $x_{n+1}=r x_n(1-x_n)$. With $r=2$, many starting values move toward the same fixed point; other parameter choices produce very different behavior. Even before proving anything, there are several questions to separate. Does one orbit converge? Do nearby orbits stay close? Which sets remain invariant? What proportion of time does a typical orbit spend in a specified region? Dynamical systems connects these questions, but the methods needed for stability and for long-term statistics are different.

For a first project, use Gerald Teschl's [Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf), the author-posted preliminary version. Chapter 10 begins with the logistic equation and develops fixed and periodic points. Solve the fixed-point equation yourself, then compute the derivative at each fixed point and investigate what it predicts. Keep the parameter and initial value explicit. A finite list of iterates can suggest an attracting cycle; showing that a neighborhood is carried closer to that cycle requires an argument. The distinction becomes especially important near a parameter where stability changes.

A reader entering through discrete maps can begin there without reading every earlier chapter on differential equations. Calculus, proof-based real analysis, and linear algebra supply the first tools. Check whether you can use the mean value theorem to prove contraction near a fixed point when the derivative has absolute value less than one. If you already know local stability and periodic orbits, sample those exercises and move to Chapter 11 on one-dimensional dynamics and symbolic descriptions. Review metric spaces and compactness when limit sets and continuity arguments become central.

Flows provide another entrance. If your motivating example is a pendulum or a population governed by a differential equation, read Teschl's Sections 1.3–1.5, the existence and uniqueness material in Chapter 2, and Chapter 6 on flows, invariant sets, and stability. An explicit solution is sometimes available, but a phase portrait can answer qualitative questions even when a formula is not. This branch also explains why the existence interval and uniqueness hypotheses belong in the discussion: before asking where an orbit goes, establish that the evolution rule defines it. You can postpone specialized boundary-value material when it does not support your chosen project.

The measurable branch changes the emphasis from individual trajectories to distributions of trajectories. Charles Walkden's [Ergodic Theory](https://personalpages.manchester.ac.uk/staff/charles.walkden/ergodic-theory/ergodic_theory.pdf) notes offer a route through uniform distribution, invariant measures, ergodicity, recurrence, and Birkhoff's theorem. Begin with Sections 1–4 and work with a circle rotation. A rational rotation gives finite periodic orbits; an irrational rotation raises questions about visits to intervals. Before Sections 5 and 9–10, become comfortable with sigma-algebras, integration, and statements holding almost everywhere. Functional analysis can support operator methods later, but it need not delay the first examples.

Use the formula $\mu(T^{-1}A)=\mu(A)$ to check that a proposed measure is invariant. Then ask the separate question of ergodicity. An invariant measure alone does not force time averages to agree with one global space average. Walkden's Section 10 states the general Birkhoff theorem using conditional expectation onto invariant information, followed by the ergodic specialization. Read the conclusion with its integrability and almost-everywhere qualifications intact. Similarly, recurrence does not mean that every trajectory returns to its exact starting point, nor does a visually irregular orbit by itself establish a chosen definition of chaos.

A good stopping point for this route is a comparison of two systems using explicit orbits, invariant sets, and an invariant measure where available. From there, follow stability and bifurcation toward smooth dynamics, coding toward symbolic dynamics, orbit averages toward ergodic theory, or Hamiltonian examples toward symplectic geometry. Carry one worked system into the new subject. It will show which extra structure the new language remembers and which new questions it makes possible.

combinatorics.body:
How many edges can a graph on $n$ vertices have if it contains no triangle? A complete bipartite graph with two nearly equal parts gives $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ edges. The difficult half is proving that every triangle-free graph satisfies the same bound. This is an extremal question: a construction gives a lower bound, and an argument excluding all better constructions gives an upper bound. Combinatorics also asks for exact counts, efficient constructions, and the existence of objects too complicated to specify directly. Those questions share examples, but they reward different methods.

For a broad undergraduate starting point, take Mitchel T. Keller and William T. Trotter's [Applied Combinatorics](https://rellek.net/book-2016/), using the 2016 HTML edition for the chapter numbering here. Work through Chapter 2 on strings, sets, and binomial coefficients, then Chapter 5 on graphs. Section 2.4, Combinatorial Proofs, is especially useful: explain an identity by describing what its two sides count. You should be able to name the objects, explain the counting rule, and justify that nothing is omitted or counted twice. Algebraic simplification can check an answer, but it does not supply those explanations.

Start with induction, finite sets, and a willingness to write precise arguments. You do not need to complete real analysis or abstract algebra before counting subsets or proving elementary graph results. To skip the early counting material, give a bijective proof of $\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n}{n-k}$, derive a recurrence by dividing objects into disjoint cases, and prove that the sum of graph degrees equals twice the number of edges. If any step feels circular, work a few small examples and identify exactly what each side represents. Small cases are useful evidence, but agreement for several values does not establish a general identity.

Enumeration offers one continuation within Keller and Trotter. Chapters 7–9 develop inclusion-exclusion, generating functions, and recurrence equations. Count permutations with forbidden fixed points, or count strings subject to a local restriction, and translate the same problem between a recurrence and a generating function. Record initial conditions. When multiplying formal power series, explain what choosing one term from each factor means combinatorially. This habit prevents a common error: finding an elegant expression that counts a slightly different class of objects. Questions involving symmetry lead to Chapter 15 on group actions, Burnside's lemma, and Pólya enumeration; add the required group theory as you reach it.

For the opening extremal problem, an alternative next text is Yufei Zhao's [Graph Theory and Additive Combinatorics: Exploring Structure and Randomness](https://yufeizhao.com/gtacbook/gtacbook.pdf), in the author-posted manuscript. Section 1.1 proves Mantel's theorem by two methods. Read one proof, close the text, and reconstruct both the bound and the equality example. Then compare the second proof to see what information it organizes differently. This is an advanced continuation: later chapters call on algebra, analysis, linear algebra, and probability. Enter after basic graph proofs are comfortable, rather than treating the apparent simplicity of the problem statement as a measure of the whole book's difficulty.

There is also an existence route. Keller and Trotter's Chapter 11 introduces Ramsey theory and the probabilistic method. A random construction can prove that an object exists even when no particular outcome has been selected. Begin by calculating an expectation or bounding the probability that a bad event occurs. Identify the probability space and justify every use of independence; linearity of expectation itself does not require independent summands. Elementary probability is enough for initial examples, while stronger concentration tools become useful for later problems.

Choose further tools by the obstruction in front of you. Linear algebra helps with ranks, eigenvalues, and incidence structures; group actions organize symmetry; probability helps build examples; analytic estimates control asymptotic counts. Zhao's later additive chapters connect equations in sets of integers with structural and random behavior. Keep exact answers separate from asymptotic estimates, and existence separate from efficient construction. A strong next project is one problem solved in two ways, with a written explanation of why each method succeeds and what it might generalize to.

higher-categories.body:
Take two continuous paths that have the same endpoints. They may be different as functions but deformable into one another while their endpoints stay fixed. We can identify them by passing to homotopy classes, or retain the deformation as additional data. Once we retain it, we can ask about deformations between deformations. Higher category theory supplies ways to organize this information while still composing maps. The motivation is concrete: replacing everything by equivalence classes can discard relationships that later constructions need. Learning the subject means understanding how those relationships are encoded and made coherent.

Begin with ordinary category theory in Emily Riehl's [Category Theory in Context](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/context.pdf). Chapters 1–4 provide the main spine: categories and functors, natural transformations, representability and Yoneda, limits, and adjunctions. Keep a familiar construction beside each definition. For example, the product of two vector spaces has projection maps through which every pair of linear maps from a third space factors uniquely. Verify that assertion before calling the product a limit. The point of a universal property is that it tells you how to use a construction and compare it with another candidate.

The useful preparation is a stock of examples from linear algebra, groups, rings, or topology, together with confidence proving statements about maps. You can start with one or two of these subjects and expand your examples as needed. To skip the introductory categorical material, construct a natural transformation, prove a simple universal property, and explain an adjunction through its hom-set bijection, including naturality. Merely recognizing the diagrams is a weaker test. If Yoneda feels detached from everything else, calculate a representable functor on a small category and work out what a natural transformation from it actually determines.

The next bridge should involve topology or homological algebra with computations. Paths and homotopies make higher morphisms visible; chain complexes make equivalences and derived constructions useful. Depending on your destination, review fundamental groups and basic homotopy, or work through chain maps, chain homotopies, and homology. These are alternative sources of motivation, not instructions to finish every course before looking ahead. What matters is being able to explain one example where preserving extra homotopical information changes the mathematical question.

Riehl's [A Leisurely Introduction to Simplicial Sets](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/ssets.pdf) offers a short, concrete entry into one language for that information. Study the simplex category and face and degeneracy maps, then the nerve of a category and the singular complex of a space. Draw the simplices in low dimensions. In the nerve, a pair of composable arrows determines a triangle expressing composition. Section 5 reaches Kan complexes and quasi-categories; the difference between filling every horn and filling inner horns distinguishes two important kinds of structure. Short length does not remove the need to check the definitions on examples.

For deeper study, Emily Riehl and Dominic Verity's [Elements of ∞-Category Theory](https://emilyriehl.github.io/files/elements.pdf) develops an approach using infinity-cosmoi and their homotopy 2-categories. Read the preface to understand the aim, then Section 1.1 on quasi-categories before proceeding to the axiomatic framework. This is a later text, with substantial categorical and homotopical demands. A concrete simplicial route and this more axiomatic route emphasize different work: the former makes the encoding visible, while the latter develops arguments that apply across several models. Choose according to the examples and constructions you want to study.

Keep equality, isomorphism, equivalence, and homotopy separate. A diagram that commutes up to a chosen homotopy contains data beyond an assertion that its composites represent the same homotopy class; compatibility among such choices creates further questions. Also specify which higher categories you mean: in an $(\infty,1)$-category, morphisms above dimension one are invertible in the appropriate higher sense. After the foundations, algebraic examples can lead toward stable categories and derived algebra, while geometric examples can lead toward spaces, descent, and higher stacks. Carry an explicit example through each change of language, and check what the new framework preserves before adopting its general vocabulary.
